analysis.one_liner: Waives federal royalties on new deep-water offshore oil and gas leases until producers recoup their investment.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it drew no cosponsors and died after a single committee hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how the federal government charges oil and gas companies that drill in deep water on the Outer Continental Shelf. Normally companies pay the government a share (a royalty) of what they pump from federal waters. The bill would let those companies skip the royalty entirely — on leases in water 200 meters deep or deeper — until they have recovered their exploration and development costs from sales, unless crude prices top $34 a barrel for two straight quarters. Deep water is where most new offshore drilling was headed, so the change would shield a growing share of offshore production from royalty payments.
analysis.who_benefits: Deep-water oil and gas producers. They could pump from federal waters for years without paying royalties, deferring payment until their exploration and development costs were recovered (bonus bids they paid for the leases don't count toward that total). The only off-switch is a price trigger: no relief in any year when West Texas Intermediate crude averages over $34 a barrel for two consecutive quarters, with that threshold rising with inflation after 1993. States' royalty shares would not be reduced, so the loss falls on the federal Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Deep-water offshore oil and gas producers

how_it_helps.text: Producers of leases in water 200 meters or deeper would pay no federal royalties until their post-lease exploration costs and development costs were recovered out of lease proceeds.
Bonus bids paid to win the lease would not count toward the recovered-cost total, so relief would last longer.

The bill's stated purpose is national energy security through encouraging domestic deep-water production, and it directs the Interior Secretary to write implementing rules within 120 days of enactment.
Payments owed to states under the act would be unaffected, so the revenue loss would land on the federal government, not state governments.

The relief would switch off for any calendar year in which the average daily NYMEX price for West Texas Intermediate crude exceeded $34 per barrel for two consecutive quarters, with the threshold indexed to inflation after 1993.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — meaning taxpayers — would forgo royalty revenue on every barrel pumped from deep-water federal leases until each operator recouped its investment. Because deep water was where new offshore production was expanding, the deferred royalties could cover a large and growing share of offshore output for years. The public would also bear the cost of rules to administer the cost-recovery accounting.

drawbacks.text: Federal royalty revenue would be deferred for years on new deep-water leases, the exact production the government was set to collect on, shrinking what the public receives for resources it owns.

The cost-recovery formula only counts exploration and development spending, not the bonus bids companies paid to win leases, which stretches the royalty-free period and makes the accounting favorable to producers.

Extra production incentives could push more drilling into increasingly deep, harder-to-respond-to offshore waters, where spills are costlier to contain; the bill contains no additional safety or environmental provisions.
The $34-per-barrel trigger, indexed to inflation, is set well above typical early-1990s crude prices, so in practice relief would be available nearly always unless prices spiked.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit case rests on the bill's own premise: cheaper royalty treatment would pull more deep-water drilling to U.S. federal waters, adding domestic supply and energy security. The cost case is stronger on the numbers: the public would give up royalties for years on the fastest-growing category of offshore production, and it is doubtful that operators deciding where to drill multibillion-dollar projects needed more than the favorable lease terms they already had. A deferral styled as temporary becomes long-lived when the price trigger sits far above the market price.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, got one hearing in August 1992, and then sat there while the two-year Congress ended in January 1993 with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Bennett Johnston, a Louisiana Democrat, introduced the bill on August 4, 1992, and it was read twice and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
The committee held hearings on the bill on August 11, 1992, printed as S.Hrg. 102-990.
No cosponsors signed on, the committee never reported the bill, and the Senate never voted on it before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers and the federal Treasury: no royalties were ever deferred, so the government kept collecting its share of deep-water production. Producers gained nothing because the bill never moved.

for.name: Sen. J. Bennett Johnston
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-LA); bill sponsor and chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as the committee's chair, held a hearing on it in August 1992; the committee never reported it to the floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill but never reported it out, leaving it without a path to a Senate vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors and no votes recorded, there is no evidence of either party organizing for or against the bill; it simply never advanced.

industries.industry: Deep-water offshore oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill would let them defer federal royalties on new deep-water leases until they recovered exploration and development costs, with a price trigger set high enough ($34/barrel, inflation-indexed) that relief would rarely switch off. Their gain would come directly out of the public's share of production from federally owned waters. The bill never advanced, so they gained nothing.

Every barrel pumped royalty-free under a cost-recovery deferral would be revenue the government forgoes; state payments would be untouched, so the hit falls on federal coffers. The bill died, so no revenue was lost.
